quote.text: A society grows great when old men plant trees in whose shade they shall never sit.
quote.author: Greek proverb

stories.kicker: The Good Life · The Everyday Speedmaster
stories.headline: A Moonwatch Face on a Watch You Can Actually Wear Daily
stories.dek: Omega has refreshed the 38-millimetre Speedmaster, and the hands-on verdicts have clustered this week. It is the accessible, wear-anywhere entry to the line — and it comes with an asterisk the enthusiasts will make sure you read: this is an automatic that looks like the watch that went to the Moon, not the watch that went to the Moon.

stories.headline: The Tree You Keep Small for Longer Than You Will Be Alive
stories.dek: Bonsai is not a plant you buy; it is a practice you take up — an ordinary tree kept miniature and made to read as an ancient one, over decades of pruning and patience. This is the weekend's deepest descent: a world of grail tools, four-figure pots, an imported clay whose price keeps doubling, and the honest admission that you will kill your first ten trees.

stories.headline: A Five-Minute Train Under the Strait Moves Toward Opening
stories.dek: The weekend's travel news is close to home: the Johor Bahru–Singapore rail link enters systems testing, still tracking a year-end target, promising a five-minute crossing of a causeway that can swallow an hour. Plus a genuinely new China route, Europe's border system going live, and the ski pipeline for the winter after this one.

stories.kicker: The World · The Strait of Hormuz
stories.headline: Six Months Shut. Now Tehran Names Its Price.
stories.dek: The world's most important oil chokepoint has been closed to routine commercial shipping for roughly half a year — the longest such closure on record. This weekend Iran did not reopen it. It put a written list of conditions on the table, drew a corridor through Omani water it has yet to use, and received a third mediator in a week. Washington's answer: the strait is already open.

stories.headline: The Help Arrives the Same Month the Bill Does
stories.dek: This is the weekend the cost-of-living support lands in bank accounts — four to six hundred dollars a person, plus vouchers. It arrives against a record power tariff and a core inflation that ticked up, not down. A study out this week says the squeeze now reaches even the comfortable. The relief is real; so is the arithmetic it is trying to outrun.

stories.kicker: The Atelier · Wallets & Small Leather Goods
stories.headline: The Wallet, From the Hide Up
stories.dek: A wallet is the one leather object you touch every day and replace least often — so it is the purest test of the desk's ethos. Learn four things — grain, tannage, edge, stitch — and you can judge any wallet cold, and see that most "designer" bifolds are eighty-dollar factory goods wearing a four-hundred-dollar name.

stories.headline: A Ninety-Six-Billion-Dollar Quarter, and a Reach for the Open World's Front Door
stories.dek: Nvidia beat its own guidance by five billion dollars and guided the next quarter higher still — then the stock fell. The same week, it is reported, still unsigned, to be buying Hugging Face, the hub that hosts the very open models the home-lab reader downloads. A record, and a quiet act of vertical integration underneath it.

stories.headline: The Big Weights Stayed Locked. The Smaller, Stranger One Opened.
stories.dek: Zhipu's flagship GLM-5.3 missed its staged open-weights date on cyber-risk grounds. But the same week it surprise-dropped GLM-5.3-Flash: 320 billion parameters, natively multimodal, a million-token context, and the most permissive licence there is. The catch for a home rig is not the graphics card — it is the memory, and the fork of the software you run it on.

stories.kicker: The Kit · The Analogue Way In
stories.headline: Pro-Ject Puts Bluetooth on Its Best Cheap Deck. Should It Have?
stories.dek: The E1.2 is the turntable most people are pointed to when they ask where to start with vinyl. Pro-Ject's new BT version adds a wireless transmitter so it can drive a speaker across the room — a genuinely useful trick, and a slightly heretical one on an object whose whole point is a wire and a needle.

stories.headline: Spider-Man Holds a Fourth Weekend; a Record Splits the Fans From the Critics by a Hair
stories.dek: The box office is a story of a hold, not a surge — the web-slinger easing toward two-and-a-quarter billion while a new horror opens behind it. And Phoebe Bridgers' album, universally praised by critics, opens a small, real gap with the people actually streaming it — a three-point argument about a sixteen-track runtime.

stories.kicker: The Family Desk · The Hinge Year
stories.headline: Twelve Is a Sensitive Window. Spend It Coaching, Not Policing.
stories.dek: Your daughter is twelve, in Secondary One, and the developmental research keeps landing on the same point: early adolescence is a window when habits set unusually hard — which is an argument for building routines with her now, and against the instinct to install another app that watches her.

stories.headline: A New Chair Tells the Market: The Work on Inflation Is Not Done
stories.dek: Kevin Warsh used his first Jackson Hole keynote to answer the doves, not to reassure them — no forward guidance, a firm reassertion of the two-per-cent target, and a warning that summer's data does not show underlying inflation improving. The market heard it and repriced toward a hike. Gold gave back part of its record; the dollar and the front end firmed.

stories.headline: Two Hours of Lifting a Week — and Not Much More
stories.dek: The longevity data keeps pointing at a specific, achievable dose of strength training: roughly ninety minutes to two hours a week, best paired with cardio. The number is oddly precise and oddly modest — which is the good news, and the asterisk is who got measured.

stories.headline: A Stacked October at Home, and a Kyushu November Worth the Flight
stories.dek: The home calendar tightens around the first-ever Singapore Sprint; Tokyo Game Show turns thirty; and a single Fukuoka trip in November can pair grand sumo with a forest of digital light. Book the fast-movers now.

stories.headline: Guilty, By the Can
stories.dek: The most abstemious generation in modern Japanese memory — barely drinking, barely smoking, starving its own budget to feed a tax-free investment account — is pouring money into the one corner of the food business branded explicitly as sin. The fastest-selling soft drink of the era is literally called Guilty. That is not a marketing accident. It is a national mood in six hundred millilitres.
